summary:
Karl Dietrich Bracher (1922–2016) was a German political scientist and historian best known for arguing that the Weimar Republic collapsed through choices by political leaders, not through inevitable forces.

Born in Stuttgart, Bracher served in the Wehrmacht and was captured by U.S. forces in Tunisia in 1943. He was held at Camp Concordia, Kansas, until 1945. He earned a doctorate in classics at Tübingen in 1948, studied at Harvard in 1949–50, taught at the Free University of Berlin from 1950 to 1958 and at Bonn from 1959 to 1987, and co-published the *Vierteljahrshefte für Zeitgeschichte* from 1978. He married Dorothee Schleicher, Dietrich Bonhoeffer’s niece, in 1951; they had two children. He died in 2016, aged 94.

Bracher’s central concern was how to protect democracy. He championed human rights, pluralism, constitutional government, and alignment with the democratic West, arguing that democracy depends on an engaged public.

His best-known book, *The Disintegration of the Weimar Republic* (1955), rejected explanations that blamed the collapse on Germany’s historical “special path,” Marxist claims of a capitalist conspiracy, the Treaty of Versailles, or fate. Bracher instead traced it to deliberate political decisions. He argued that presidential government, begun under Heinrich Brüning in 1930, weakened democracy by governing through emergency powers rather than parliament. He described the breakdown in three stages: democratic “loss of power” under Brüning, a “power vacuum” under Franz von Papen and Kurt von Schleicher, and the Nazis’ seizure of power in 1933. He also blamed a politicized judiciary for lenient treatment of right-wing political crimes.

Bracher disputed conservative historian Werner Conze’s claim that presidential government was an unavoidable response to crisis and a temporary effort to save democracy. Bracher argued that it was planned well before the Great Depression as a move toward right-wing rule outside parliament. Brüning’s memoirs, published in 1970, largely supported that interpretation. Bracher also faulted Social Democrats for failing to resist Papen’s 1932 coup against Prussia’s elected government, arguing that resistance could have preserved democratic morale even if it failed. Later research, historian Eberhard Kolb wrote, supported Bracher’s account of Brüning.

Bracher rejected the idea that Germany followed an inevitable Sonderweg, but argued that a distinctive German political mentality—shaped by völkisch ideas and opposition to democracy—helped make Nazism possible. In *The National Socialist Seizure of Power* (1960), written with Wolfgang Sauer and Gerhard Schulz, he documented the Nazis’ consolidation of control in 1933–34. His 1969 *The German Dictatorship* treated Nazi Germany as a totalitarian regime produced by human actions. Bracher opposed both Ernst Nolte’s theory of generic fascism and Marxist accounts that made Nazi leaders instruments of business interests. He argued that Nazi ideology and political power took precedence over economic interests, and that totalitarianism should be studied empirically rather than through rigid models. He also criticized historians who portrayed Hitler as a weak dictator.
